artworks.title: Miniature boots belonging to Charles S. Stratton
artworks.description:
Pair of miniature boots in brown and black leather, with dark yellow leather around the top openings, originally worn by Charles S. Stratton. Stratton is better known by his stage name, "General Tom Thumb." The foot size is among the smallest of Stratton's footwear in the museum's collection, just 5 1/2 inches long, indicating that these were worn when he was still young. Stratton gew slowly over the course of his life, and his later footwear is of a larger size. Most likely this pair dates from the mid-1840s to 1850s, and may have been purchased when Stratton was touring in the U. S., as the maker, Leonard Benkert, was located at No. 209 Chestnut Street in Philadelphia. The squared-toed boots with leather soles and stacked leather heels have blue and white pull-on straps stitched inside. The uppers and soles reveal a lot of wear, with the heels worn down at the back and part of the soles missing (probably a much later loss as the leather became brittle). The comparison to a U. S. penny provides scale, showing both the short length and the narrowness of the foot. The boots are 6 1/2 inches tall.

artworks.title: Miniature tall boot belonging to Charles S. Stratton
artworks.description:
Miniature tall boot made of leather that belonged to Charles S. Stratton, better known by his stage name, "General Tom Thumb." The boot was likely part of Stratton's Napoleon costume, one of several characters he portrayed in performances, and the one that was his most popular. This style of boot goes over the knee at the front and on the sides, but is cut away at the back for ease of movement. The heel is short but would slightly elevate the wearer. Various photographs of Stratton portraying Napoleon show him wearing boots of this style, and he probably had several pairs like this over the years. Stratton was a little person whom Barnum made famous beginning in 1843; Barnum met Stratton when he was just shy of his fifth birthday and was less than two feet tall, having virtually ceased growing around 7 months of age. Stratton did grow very slowly over the course of his life, and was 42 inches tall at the time of his death. This boot, which measures 9 1/4 inches tall x 4 5/8 inches long x 1 1/4 inches wide, must have been worn when Stratton was still quite young, as the foot is exceptionally small. It most likely dates to the mid-1840s, early in Stratton's career, when Barnum took him on a three-year tour of Europe, with a major portion of their time spent in the British Isles. The boot has an English shoemaker's label: J. Joseph, 13 Skinner Street, Snow Hill, London. The name is stamped in gold on a rectangle of black leather that has been affixed to the rose pink leather lining. This is a single boot, missing its mate, however a match to this boot has been identified in another museum's collection. The surface of this boot is now extremely worn and fragile, and the boot straps, shown in one of the photos, are almost completely frayed into threads.

artworks.title: Replica Foot of Charles S. Stratton (Gen. Tom Thumb)
artworks.description:
Parian ware replica of Charles S. Stratton's left foot and ankle. Strattton, better known by his stage name, General Tom Thumb, was a little person promoted by showman P.T. Barnum as the "Man in Miniature." His height at age 5 was only 24 inches, but ultimately he did grow to be 42 inches tall. The object measures 2 3/4-inches tall x 3 1/2-inches long, representing the size of Stratton's foot between the1840s and 1850s. Parian ware was invented in 1845 by the Staffordshire, England, pottery firm Mintons; it is a type of bisque porcelain that imitates white marble. It has a smooth but not glassy surface. The reason for this replica's existence is unknown, perhaps in some way it functioned as a surrogate to show people how very small Stratton was, or because people wanted to see his tiny feet, which as a performer in costume, would not have been exposed. Since Parian ware was a new thing at the time Stratton was touring in England with P. T. Barnum (1844-1846 and again in 1856-1857), the replica might possibly have been made to show off the character and quality of the material with its ability to render a high level of detail, something that common earthenware ceramics could not. Unfortunately, this piece has sustained considerable damage over time; the old repairs are quite visible in some views.

artworks.title: Bicorn hat belonging to Charles S. Stratton
artworks.description:
Miniature bicorn hat of felted wool worn by Charles S. Stratton as part of his Napoleon costume. Stratton, a performer employed by P. T. Barnum, is better known by his stage name, "General Tom Thumb." He played a wide variety of character roles; among them his Napoleon Bonaparte character was his most famous. Surviving photographs document Strattton's performances as the French general over a period of many years during which time Stratton's costumes changed, as he grew somewhat taller and bigger. The size of this silk-lined hat, 5 inches high x 14 inches long, suggests it was worn by Stratton when he was a teen or adult, as it would be too large for him when a young child. The hat is damaged along one of the top edges, and is missing the cockade, a decorative element that would have been attached on the front side. The Barnum Museum owns other items pertaining to Stratton's Napoleon, including a wool jacket, however this particular hat and the jacket were not necessarily worn together.

artworks.title: Nautical spyglass owned by Charles S. Stratton
artworks.description:
Nautical spyglass or telescope that belonged to Charles S. Stratton, better known by his stage name, General Tom Thumb. The cylindrical object is made of brass and glass, and has an outer covering of brown leather, with two protective rings of finely twisted cord. Some of the brass rings appear to have been "japanned" or blackened. When closed the spyglass measures 6 inches long; fully extended, it measures 13.25 inches. Although the spyglass is small, it is a standard size, not a miniature version custom made for Stratton, who was a little person. There are two tubes that pull out from the main cylinder, hence this is called a "two-draw" spyglass. The spyglass was very likely acquired by Stratton who, in his mid-thirties, purchased a racing yacht called the Maggie B. It was acquired after his 1872 world tour, with Stratton having bought it from a man named Henry R. Bishop, with the intent to clean it up and use it for racing. Charles himself worked the tiller, and apparently he invited Barnum and his family onto the vessel, as Barnum's grandson Clinton Seeley recalled being on it when he was a child. The Barnum Museum also owns two nautical compasses used by Stratton on his yachts. Charles S. Stratton (January 4, 1838 - July 15, 1883) was an entertainer who got his start with P. T. artworks.title: Horseshoe belonging to one of Charles S. Stratton's ponies
artworks.description:
Pony horseshoe believed to have been worn by one of the miniature horses or ponies who drew the show carriage of Charles S. Stratton, better known by his stage name, General Tom Thumb. Tom Thumb's miniature "equipage" (turnout of carriage, coachman, and ponies) is featured in many of the souvenirs and advertisements promoting his celebrity. Queen Victoria famously presented Stratton with a custom-made miniature coach and ponies, though her gift was not the only such carriage made for him. Stratton's miniature carriages were most likely pulled by Shetland ponies, which are very small, ranging in height at the withers (shoulders) between 28 and 46 inches. They are a hardy breed known for strength and intelligence, and were traditionally bred to pull carts and small wagons, and as pack animals. This U-shaped iron shoe, just 3 inches long by 2 3/16 inches wide, was probably kept as a memento of one of the ponies. The shoe is flat on one side and on the opposite side has grooves near the edge and round indentations near the ends.
Charles S. Stratton (January 4, 1838- July 15, 1883), known as General Tom Thumb, was an entertainer and Bridgeport Conn. native who got his start with P.T. Barnum in 1842. Stratton's parents signed him with Barnum at age 4, as exhibiting those with dwarfism was lucrative at the time. Stratton took quickly to performing, and he entertained audiences worldwide, including nobility such as Queen Victoria. Stratton married fellow performer M. Lavinia Warren and the two had a happy marriage. Stratton's performances brought him renown as a celebrity, perhaps one of the biggest at the time, and he and Warren were able to live comfortably when not working. On July 15, 1883, Stratton suffered a stroke and passed away. He is buried at Mountain Grove Cemetery in Bridgeport, Connecticut, with his wife beside him.

artworks.title: Pair of stockings belonging to M. Lavinia Warren
artworks.description:
Pair of knitted silk stockings in pale pink, worn by M. Lavinia Warren during the 1860s, 1870s, or early 1880s. Lavinia Warren is better known as "Mrs. General Tom Thumb," and more properly as Mrs. Charles S. Stratton. Both Lavinia and her husband were celebrity performers employed and promoted by P. T. Barnum, as well as touring on their own. Part of their appeal was their short stature, as Lavinia and Charles were little people, as well as capable and skilled performers. Lavinia was married to Stratton from 1863 until his death in 1883, and then remarried two years later to Primo Magri. As a result, we know from the initials “L.W.S.” that are knit into the upper part of each stocking means that they date from the time of her first marriage. Measuring 18 inches high, the stockings are miniature versions of those worn by normal-sized women in the 1800s. Silk stockings were generally considered "for best," while cotton or wool stockings were usual for everyday wear.
Mercy Lavinia Warren (nee Bump) Stratton (October 31, 1841 - November 25, 1919), then Mercy Lavinia Magri, was a well known entertainer during the latter half of the 1800s. She first became a schoolteacher, but at the encouragement of a relative, she began her career as a performer on a river boat (Spaulding & Rogers Boat Shows); exhibiting little people (people with dwarfism) was profitable at the time. Warren signed with showman P. T. Barnum when she was 21. In December of 1862, Charles S. Stratton (General Tom Thumb) began courting Lavinia and their whirlwind romance led to their famed marriage, "The Fairy Wedding," just two months later on February 10, 1863, with Lavinia's younger sister, Minnie Warren as bridesmaid and "Commodore Nutt" as best man. The Strattons worked and toured together as celebrities, and had a happy marriage. Following Stratton’s death in 1883, Warren married Primo Magri, an Italian entertainer of a similar stature, on April 6, 1885. Magri and Warren toured, and also operated a roadside stand in Middleboro, Massachusetts, her home town. Warren died at age 78 on November 25, 1919. She is buried beside Stratton at Mountain Grove Cemetery in Bridgeport, Connecticut.

artworks.title: Garnet ring belonging to Charles S. Stratton
artworks.description:
Tiny gold metal ring set with faceted garnets, worn by Charles S. Stratton, better known by his stage name, General Tom Thumb. The slender, delicate ring features a large garnet in the center, flanked by two smaller ones. The diameter is just over 1/2 inch (0.625") and the band itself is thin and fragile and appears to have been repaired; this ring would not have held up well to daily wear. Based upon the ring's size it is presumed to have been worn when he was young, probably in the 1840s and/or 1850s. An oil portrait of Stratton in the Barnum Museum's collection, painted when he was six years old, shows him with rings on two fingers, however neither match this one. The maker of this ring is unknown. For years it has been stored in a small green box with an old (though not original) label glued to the lid. Charles S. Stratton (January 4, 1838 - July 15, 1883), known as General Tom Thumb, was an entertainer and Bridgeport Conn. native who got his start with P.T. Barnum in 1842. Stratton's parents signed him with Barnum at age 4, as exhibiting those with dwarfism was lucrative at the time. Stratton took quickly to performing, and he entertained audiences worldwide, including nobility such as Queen Victoria. Stratton married fellow performer M. Lavinia Warren and the two had a happy marriage. Stratton's performances brought him renown as a celebrity, perhaps one of the biggest at the time, and he and Warren were able to live comfortably when not working. On 15 July 1883, Stratton suffered a stroke and passed away. He is buried at Mountain Grove Cemetery in Bridgeport, Connecticut, with his wife beside him.

artworks.title: Receipt to Charles S. Stratton from Sammis & Fairchild Clothiers, 1872
artworks.description:
Receipt for the purchase of a yachting suit from Sammis & Fairchild Clothiers in Bridgeport, Connecticut. The purchaser was Charles S. Stratton, better known by his stage name, "General Tom Thumb." The receipt is dated August 6, 1872. The yachting suit cost $30 and must have been custom-made to fit Stratton's small stature, though probably all such suits would have been individually tailored at that time. During the 1870s, Stratton owned two yachts, which he sailed on Long Island Sound and used in racing competitions. Sammis & Fairchild Clothiers was located at 227 Main Street in downtown Bridgeport.
Charles S. Stratton (January 4, 1838 - July 15, 1883) was an entertainer who got his start with P. T. Barnum in the early 1840s. Stratton's parents signed him with Barnum when the boy was barely five years old. The family went to live in New York City where Stratton performed at Barnum's American Museum, located on Broadway at Ann Street. The little boy took quickly to performing, and on tours he entertained audiences worldwide, including royalty. Stratton's performances brought him renown, becoming one of the biggest celebrities at the time, and considerable wealth. In 1863, Stratton married fellow performer and little person M. Lavinia Warren; the two had a happy marriage, and continued touring and performing. On July 15, 1883, Stratton suffered a stroke and passed away. He is buried at Mountain Grove Cemetery in Bridgeport, Connecticut.

artworks.title: A:Shiwi (Zuni) Crenellated Medicine Bowl with Black Decorative Motifs on Grey-White Background
artworks.description:
A:Shiwi (Zuni) crenellated medicine bowl. It would have held a mixture of water and corn pollen or cornmeal for ceremonial use, most likely on an altar in a kiva. The black (bee plant?) decorative motifs on the grey-white background include, Koshare (sacred clowns), serpents (probably Koo'lo'wisi, the Plumed Water Serpent, both outside and inside the bowl), clouds, rain, and the crenellations represent mountains or possibly even multi-storied Halona village, the main Zuni village which dates to pre-Hispanic times.
Object identification and additional information were provided by Dr. Jonathan Reyman, Native American anthropologist (Pueblo Specialist) and former Curator of Anthropology at the Illinois State Museum. Dr. Reyman examined the object via photographs.
In terms of its history with the Barnum Museum, this bowl was originally part of the David Pell Secor collection displayed in the early years of the Barnum Institute of Science and History, opened in 1893. The interior of the bowl features two human figures on one side and two snakes on the other.

artworks.title: Untitled
artworks.description:
A:Shiwi (Zuni) canteen with round, spherical body and short neck. The reverse of the canteen is flattened and shows the buff/brown color of the clay. It is painted black and white on one side. The black is mineral paint, and the white underlay is kaolin, a white clay generally found in the Acoma Pueblo area and imported throughout the Ancestral Pueblo area during both pre-Hispanic and post-conquest times. The main design motif appears to be a turtle, an animal sacred to the A:Shiwi. The two large lugs once held cordage for carrying the canteen which, among other uses, was taken to the fields when the people engaged in horticulture. The blackened surface of the flattened side suggests it was exposed to fire, possibly to heat the water within.
Object identification and additional information were provided by Dr. Jonathan Reyman, Native American anthropologist (Pueblo Specialist) and former Curator of Anthropology at the Illinois State Museum. Dr. Reyman examined the object via photographs.

artworks.title: Untitled
artworks.description:
Tripartite comb made out of the ivory of an unidentified mammal. Made by an unidentified Inuit tribe, the comb features a whale tail motif on the handle. According to Dr. Jonathan Reyman, Native American anthropologist (Pueblo Specialist) and former Curator of Anthropology at the Illinois State Museum, given the material and width of the teeth, this was probably used to comb out tangles from women's long and somewhat stiff hair and possibly also that of men.
Carving ivory was considered a man's skill historically, and being able to create elaborate combs was one way to demonstrate those skills. Comb designs vary from simple and straight forward to incredibly intricate.
There is debate about the appropriate term for cultures native to the northern circumpolar region. Eskimo is considered a pejorative in Canada and Greenland, but this opinion is not shared by others. The use of the word Inuit does not cover all native cultures either, as Native Alaskans do not fall strictly under the definition of Inuit. It is a complex issue, and because the Barnum Museum does not know the exact tribe that this artifact came from, the general term Northern Circumpolar people has been used in description and Inuit in its subject headings.

artworks.title: Untitled
artworks.description:
Inuit fish scaler made of bone. Its origin is with the Inuit people or other Northern Circumpolar peoples. The scaler features a wide, flat end for removing a fish's scales, and this tapers into a narrow portion that functions as a handle. There is incised geometric decoration in the middle portion and the design shows a slight amount of reddish-brown color. Sinew is now in a knot in the center of the scaler, but its original form was a loop with the purpose of slipping over the user's finger. This would keep it from being dropped which otherwise could happen frequently in working with wet or oily fish.
There is debate about the appropriate term for cultures native to the northern circumpolar region. Eskimo is considered a pejorative in Canada and Greenland, but this opinion is not shared by others. The use of the word Inuit does not cover all native cultures either, as Native Alaskans do not fall strictly under the definition of Inuit. It is a complex issue, and because the Barnum Museum does not know the exact tribe that this artifact came from, the general term Northern Circumpolar people has been used in description and Inuit in its subject headings.
According to Dr. Jonathan Reyman, Native American anthropologist (Pueblo Specialist) and former Curator of Anthropology at the Illinois State Museum, the item dates to early 19th century. Later metal knives were more commonly used, although bone knives continued in use into the 20th century to cut snow blocks for igloos.

artworks.title: Untitled
artworks.description:
Pair of ear spools or labrets. Ear spools are placed in elongated or widened ear lobes while labrets are placed just below the lower lip. It is known that these are from an Inuit culture, but the specific tribe has never been identified. Without knowing the exact tribe of origin, the meaning of this pair of ornaments is obscured. It is known that body modification ornaments, particularly labret ornaments, were used by various Inuit peoples to communicate a broad variety of messages that could include social affiliation, and ranks within a tribe, or a desire for personal adornment.
According to Dr. Jonathan Reyman, Native American anthropologist (Pueblo Specialist) and former Curator of Anthropology at the Illinois State Museum, these are more likely ear spools (not labrets as originally identified) placed in elongated or widened ear lobes. They look like they are grey soapstone.

artworks.title: Barnum and Bailey Greatest Show on Earth letterhead
artworks.description:
Stationery for Barnum and Bailey's Greatest Show on Earth featuring portraits of both men on the left and right side of the header respectively. Dates from the 1900s.
Barnum is best known for his involvement with the circus that still bears his name, but his circus ventures came about when he was in his 60s. The first show was called P.T. Barnum’s Grand Traveling Museum, Menagerie, Caravan and Circus. Railroads propelled the circus to success, making it easier to reach a number of locations, and the intake was significant. Barnum then opened the New York Hippodrome with similar acts. In the 1880s, he encountered competition from other circuses. A merger between Barnum’s show the Great London Show of Cooper, Bailey, and Hutchinson formed the Barnum and London Circus. Negotiations in 1887 formed the Barnum and Bailey circus. The name remained until 1919 when it became the Ringling Brothers and Barnum and Bailey circus.

artworks.title: Ironstone pudding mold with elephant
artworks.description:
Ceramic pudding mold with an elephant silhouette impressed into the bottom of the mold, most likely representing Jumbo, the large-earred African elephant made famous by P. T. Barnum. (When the pudding is finished and flipped over to release it from the mold, the "bottom" becomes the top of the pudding. Thus the slightly dimensional elephant decorates the top of the pudding.) The off-white color mold is made of a sturdy type of earthenware called "ironstone," so named for its durability, not because there is iron in the material. Ironstone was popular for everyday kitchen items and dinnerware in the 1800s and early 1900s The mold may date from 1882 to 1885 when Jumbo was in North America and, with Barnum's widespread promotion, spawned the craze for all things elephant ("Jumbomania"). The mold may have been made in America, or imported from England, where there were many potteries in Staffordshire producing ironstone items. If English, the mold may be earlier, dating to the 1870s or the early 1880s when Jumbo was a resident of the London Zoo. In addition to the elephant design, the mold is fluted all around the interior to create a very attractive pudding. The exterior is smooth, save for slight indentations, and overall gives the appearance of an oval bowl.
In the 1700s and 1800s, the word "pudding" referred to a broad range of foods, both savory and sweet. Puddings, jellies and other molded desserts were very popular in Victorian cookery, so there was a large market for fancy and unusual molds to create elegant looking desserts.
Jumbo the Elephant (ca. 1861 - September 15, 1885) was an unusually tall African elephant best known for his time as an attraction in the London Zoological Gardens, and as a part of P.T. Barnum's circus from 1882 to his untimely death in 1885. His sale by the London Zoo to Barnum and his partners prompted a great public outcry in England, but Barnum used even negative publicity to his advantage. Sent to America in a very large crate with his long-time keeper Matthew Scott, Jumbo toured cities and towns in the United States and Canada as part of Barnum's circus. He was not trained to perform like the Asian species of elephant in circuses; he only needed to be his huge, "jumbo" self to attract the crowds. Sadly, Jumbo was killed by a train in St. Thomas, Ontario, Canada, on September 15, 1885, as he was returning from an evening performance, walking on the railroad tracks. Barnum had the elephant's hide and bones mounted separately by Ward's Scientific of Rochester, New York. The pair were exhibited under circus tents as "Double Jumbo" for two or three years after Jumbo's death. The stuffed hide was then given to Tufts College (now Tufts University), where Barnum served on the founding Board, and the bones were given to the American Museum of Natural History in New York City, where they remain today. The mounted hide was lost to fire in the mid-1970s.

artworks.title: Pitcher featuring Jumbo the elephant
artworks.description:
Earthenware pitcher featuring Jumbo, an African elephant who became an international celebrity in the late 1800s. This pitcher, likely used to serve water, was a mass-market item, probably sold at the height of Jumbo's popularity in the 1870s and 1880s. Jumbo appears on both sides of the pitcher, with his name beneath. The handle is made to resemble a branch or woody vine, and where it joins the body of the pitcher, there is a cluster of leaves with a large white (or unpainted) flower resembling a morning glory. The painting appears to have been hastily done, which reflects its level of quality as a mass-market product. Jumbo having been painted brown rather than the grey color of an elephant, is consistent with typical colors used in Majolica pottery. There is no maker mark on the bottom, and it is unknown if this is was made in England or America. If English, it may date from about 1865 to the early 1880s when Jumbo lived at the London Zoo. If American, it may date from 1882 or later, when Jumbo was in North America.
This particular pitcher is known as Majolica ware, an extremely popular style of pottery in the 1800s. To create pieces, material was cast in a mold, and the features were then painted with colored lead glazes. The item was then fired to produce the hard shiny finish and translucent appearance.
Jumbo (about 1861-September 15, 1885) grew to be an unusually tall African elephant, about 11 1/2 feet tall at the time of his death. He was captured in Sudan when still very young, and was rather sickly while growing up. He became a main attraction at the London Zoo as the "Children's Giant Pet, " over the years, giving rides around the park to thousands of children. His sale from the London Zoo to Barnum and his partners prompted a great public outcry in England, but in typical Barnum fashion, Barnum used the negative publicity to his advantage. Jumbo arrived in America in April 1882, and thereafter was part of the circus, touring the United States and southern Canada. His arrival was widely promoted, as were his appearances in the shows. The public could not get enough of Jumbo, and manufacturers capitalized on this Jumbo-mania, producing many types of products with his name and image, while advertisers touted all kinds products with comparisons to the elephant's size or strength. Jumbo was killed by a train on September 15, 1885, while on tour in St. Thomas, Ontario, Canada. He was only a young adult elephant at age 24 or 25 years old, and his death was widely mourned. His name, however, lives on as we refer to super large items, from eggs and beverages to jet airplanes as "jumbo sized." Barnum employed a taxidermist in Rochester, New York to mount the hide and skeleton separately, to be shown for a year or two in the circus as "Double Jumbo." The mounted hide was then given to Tufts College (now Tufts University) but was lost to fire in 1975; the skeleton was given to the American Museum of Natural History in New York City where the bones remain in storage today.

artworks.title: Christening cup for Frances B. Thompson, granddaughter of P.T. Barnum
artworks.description:
Silver Christening cup given as a gift to Frances B. Thompson, daughter of Caroline and David Thompson, and the first grandchild of P. T. and Charity Barnum. Caroline was the Barnum's eldest daughter. The mug-shaped silver cup is highly decorated with engraved designs surrounding a large cartouche ("framed" area for text) that reads "Frances B. Thompson / from her Grandmother, / F. Thompson / Mch 23. 1854." She was born on December 17, 1853.
It was common for a Christening ceremony to take place two or three months after the birth of an infant, as the date of this cup suggests was the case for Frances. Silver cups, for those who could afford to make such gifts, were traditional and cherished Christening gifts; the information engraved on them also helps preserve the family history. Frances's paternal grandparents were Eli and Frances Thompson, and so she was likely named after her grandmother, though possibly also in memory of one of Caroline's sisters, also named Frances, who had died around age two.
Caroline was close with her father and went on several major trips with him during the years she was growing up. She kept diaries that document these travels. Caroline married David W. Thompson in October of 1852, and their union was happy. In addition to their daughter Frances, they had a son who was named after his famous grandfather, Phineas Taylor Barnum Thompson. Sadly, the little boy died on February 27, 1868 at age 2 years and 20 months. A silver Christening cup made by Tiffany & Co. had been given to him by P. T. Barnum, and is now privately owned. Frances married William B. Leigh in 1886, and the couple had one daughter, Nancy Barnum Leigh, who died at age 20 in 1909 and left no heirs. Frances lived to the age of 85, passing away on January 26, 1939. She was both the first and the last of P. T. Barnum's granddaughters.

artworks.title: Silver spoon holder with initials of P. T. Barnum
artworks.description:
Silver teaspoon holder, also called a spooner, engraved with P. T. Barnum's monogram. The spooner is shaped like a small vase, but with a scrolled handle on each side, similar to a trophy. Its purpose was to hold teaspoons, for use when tea was served. If the tea drinker wished to add milk and/or a sweetener to his or her cup of tea, the tea needed to be stirred, so having spoons at hand was a convenience.
From the Victorian period well into the 1900s, spooners were common for everyday family use, not just when company visited. Less costly than silver spooners were those made of patterned glass or various kinds of ceramic materials. These were often more simply shaped, cylindrical with straight sides and no handles nor footed base. The initials PTB are engraved on this spooner in the center of the upper third; beneath it, a design of grapes and grape leaves encircles the rounded midsection. Both the rim and the base have a beaded design around their perimeter. The beading on the rim distinguishes this from a drinking vessel such as a goblet. The maker of this silver spooner is unknown, as is the date of its creation, but it likely dates from around the 1850s to 1870s. Barnum frequently traveled in Europe, and over the course of his life spent a lot of time in England; his second wife was an Englishwoman. He may therefore have adopted English habits and customs of tea drinking. The Barnum Museum collection includes a large needlework tea cozy (teapot cover) that also belonged to Barnum.

artworks.title: Gothic style mantel clock with a glass panel featuring Barnum's Iranistan home
artworks.description:
Mantel or shelf clock with a steeple style top, featuring a glass panel with an image of P. T. Barnum's home, Iranistan, in Bridgeport, Connecticut. The clock is in a wood case in which the front is covered in a fine veneer (thin layer) of mahogany, a type of wood especially prized for fine furniture in the 1700s and early 1800s. This clock may date from 1848 when Barnum's home was completed, or slightly later, in the 1850s. Barnum's elaborate home was truly unique in America at the time, and he used it to market himself, as part of his "brand." Although it may seem unusual today to own a clock featuring someone else's home, in the mid-1800s this clock might have suggested to its owners' visitors that he or she kept abreast of popular interests--Barnum and his extraordinary home were "in the news." The clockworks and face are positioned in the upper half of the case, and the pendulum hangs down into the lower half. The clock face is simple and unadorned. An access door on the front allowed for weekly winding of the clock. The door has a triangular top to fit the shape of the case, and contains two glass panels, the top one being clear glass to protect the clock face, while the bottom one is decorative and hides the pendulum. The picture was created by applying a transfer print to the backside of the glass. An artist then painted over the print (also on the backside of the glass) using colors appropriate to defining the lawn, building, trees and sky. In this way, the artist did not need to do fine detail work but simply painted large areas of color, since the print supplied the "drawing" of the house. This method simplified the creation of a "reverse painting on glass" which traditionally was all painted by hand. In addition the transfer could include, as it does here along the bottom, a printed title, which eliminated the need to paint the letters (which would be in reverse) by hand. The picture is titled "Barnum's Villa." See 2013.001.001 for another example of a case clock with the same image, but a brighter variation of the painting.
P. T. Barnum's first home in his adopted city of Bridgeport, Connecticut, was located on present day Fairfield Avenue, technically part of the neighboring town of Fairfield at the time. It was heavily inspired by the Royal Pavilion in Brighton, England, which Barnum had visited in the mid-1840s. Using drawings Barnum had acquired of the Pavillion, architect Leopold Eidlitz designed the mansion in the Moorish revival style. The resemblance to the Royal Pavilion is unmistakable. The cost was $100,000 in addition to the seventeen acres of land with a conservatory and other ornate outbuildings. No photographs are known to exist, but the mansion's decor was fully described in news articles of the day. (See 2006.005.003 and 1996.009.001 for two original watercolor pictures of Iranistan.) The cause of the fire that consumed the mansion in December of 1857 was believed to be smoldering ashes from a workman's pipe. Barnum and his family were not occupying the house at the time, as repairs were being made, and the fire did not become apparent until night.

artworks.title: Decorative feature from Barnum's home, Iranistan
artworks.description:
Fanciful architectural element believed to have been saved from P. T. Barnum's home Iranistan, in Bridgeport, Connecticut. The "oriental villa," as it was described, burned to the ground in December of 1857, only a decade after it was built. This feature is the only architectural element thought to have survived, and was said to have been pulled from the building by a firefighter and saved by later generations of his family. Although it appears to be carved sandstone, it is actually made of wood painted with a gritty material to resemble the surface of reddish-brown sandstone. The element features a bearded, devilish face surrounded by leaves, creating the overall shape of an acanthus leaf. This kind of architectural element with an odd-looking face is known as a "grotesque," similar to the better known "gargoyle." Pictures of Iranistan show that there were dozens of these grotesques placed at regular intervals around the top of the ornate structure. Barnum's taste for imaginative human and animal imagery is also evident in the furniture and household decorative arts that decorated his homes.
P. T. Barnum's first home in his adopted city of Bridgeport, Connecticut, was located on present day Fairfield Avenue, technically part of the neighboring town of Fairfield at the time. It was heavily inspired by the Royal Pavilion in Brighton, England, which Barnum had visited in the mid-1840s. Using drawings Barnum had acquired of the Pavillion, architect Leopold Eidlitz designed the mansion in the Moorish revival style. The resemblance to the Royal Pavilion is unmistakable. The cost was $100,000 in addition to the seventeen acres of land with a conservatory and other ornate outbuildings. No photographs are known to exist, but the mansion's decor was fully described in news articles of the day. (See 2006.005.003 and 1996.009.001 for two original watercolor pictures of Iranistan.) The cause of the fire that consumed the mansion was believed to be smoldering ashes from a workman's pipe. Barnum and his family were not occupying the house at the time, as repairs were being made, and the fire did not become apparent until night.

artworks.title: Memorial ribbon for P. T. Barnum's funeral
artworks.description:
Black funeral ribbon worn by a City of Bridgeport government official at the funeral of P. T. Barnum. The silk ribbon is printed in silver color ink. The text at the top reads "In Memoriam." The seal of the City of Bridgeport, with its incorporation date of 1836, is beneath. Below the seal are the words, "Bridgeport City Government," and in larger letters below, "Phineas T. Barnum." The date of the funeral, April 10, 1891, is at the bottom of the ribbon.
P. T. Barnum died at his home Marina, in Bridgeport, Connecticut, on April 7, 1891, apparently from a weakened heart and late effects of a stroke. He was 80 years and 9 months old. He is thought to have suffered a stroke on November 6, 1890, from which he never fully recovered. His death was not unexpected, and he decided to have his obituary published on March 24, 1891, by the New York Tribune so that he could read it before he passed. He spent the last few weeks of his life receiving visits from friends and giving them gifts. Barnum planned his own funeral service, which was held at South Congregational Church in Bridgeport because that church had the capacity to hold the large number of mourners anticipated. Barnum himself was a member of the Universalist church in Bridgeport, and his pastor, Lewis B. Fisher, with Barnum's long-time friend, the Rev. Robert Collyer, conducted the funeral ceremony. The service reflected Barnum's Universalist faith. His coffin was carried from the church to Mountain Grove Cemetery in Bridgeport, a magnificent landscaped cemetery that he had helped create in the late 1840s.

artworks.title: Arthur Caley (Colonel Ruth Goshen) and second man
artworks.description:
Photograph of Arthur Caley also called Colonel Ruth (or Routh) Goshen, giant, with unidentified man standing beside him. Goshen (1824 – February 12, 1889), born Arthur James Caley on the Isle of Man, was most commonly known as Colonel Routh Goshen or the Arabian Giant or the Palestine Giant.
Caley is dressed in military-style clothing with a medium-toned tailcoat with light front and epaulets, white trousers, knee boots, and helmet with multiple feather plumes. He is carrying a long sword which reaches from his waist to the floor. The man with him is wearing a dark frock coat and trousers, white shirt and dark bow tie.
Inscription on the back reads "Arthur Caley, alias Colonel Ruth Goshen "The Manx Giant" "

The outline of the image is more elaborate than most, with ogee curves at the corners. The photographer is identified on the back as "A. Scidmore,[sic] Photographer Appleton, Wis." The card has a mottled blue background on both the front and back.

artworks.title: Portrait of boy and young girl
artworks.description:
Carte de visite photographic portrait of a boy and a young girl. She is wearing a light colored jacket trimmed around the edges and cuffs with a darker ribbon and her full knee-length skirt is trimmed with two rows of ribbon. She also wears a dark boater hat with light and dark ribbon hatbands. The boy is wearing a light colored suit with slightly narrower ribbon trim around lapels, edges and patch pockets on the jacket and down the side seam of the trousers. He is wearing a medium colored derby hat.
The two stand next to each other, with the girl's left hand holding the boy's right elbow, and the boy's left hand tucked into a patch pocket.
The photographer is identified on the back as "The Athenaeum Portrait Gallery. A. R. MacWilliams. Photographic Artist. 16 So. Hanover Street. (Adjoining General Post Office) Glasgow."

artworks.title: Portrait of two women in street clothes
artworks.description:
Carte de visite photographic portrait of two women wearing street clothes. They are standing next to each other, each with an elbow resting on a railing. The woman on the left is wearing a darker colored long-sleeved dress trimmed with ribbon and fringe on the bodice, the upper sleeves and to resemble an apron on the front of the skirt. She has a lace collar pinned with a brooch and her center-parted hair is in ringlets. The woman on the right is wearing a long-sleeved dress of a similar darker shade trimmed with braid on the bodice, the shoulders and cuffs of the sleeves, and down the skirt. She has a plain turned-down collar and her side-parted hair is combed back smoothly and seems to be pinned up.
The photographer is identified on the back as "The Athenaeum Portrait Gallery. A. R. MacWilliams. Photographic Artist. 16 So. Hanover Street. (Adjoining General Post Office) Glasgow."

artworks.title: Portrait of couple sword fighting
artworks.description:
Carte de visite photographic portrait of two people in acrobat's costumes holding swords and poised to fight. The figure on the left is turned partly away from the viewer. The dark long-sleeved costume is decorated with polka dots or spangles, the shorts are trimmed with fringe, and it seems to include a short cape. The woman on the right has a long-sleeved top, a pointed yoke on the front of the shorts, and a puff running around each leg. Over her left shoulder she is carrying a Union Jack flag.
The photographer is identified on the back as "The Athenaeum Portrait Gallery. A. R. MacWilliams. Photographic Artist. 16 So. Hanover Street. (Adjoining General Post Office) Glasgow."

artworks.title: Portrait of family of four acrobats
artworks.description:
Carte de visite photographic portrait of a family of four acrobats consisting of a man, a woman and two boys. The adults are wearing matching costumes of polka-dotted tops with round necklines and cap sleeves, and dark gathered shorts. The woman is also wearing a floral decorated belt with upper and lower points in the front, more recently called a waist cincher. The boys' costumes have lighter colored tops with trim around the neck, short sleeves and down the front. Their dark shorts are gathered and supplemented with a triangular drape in the front. All are wearing white tights and matching ankle-high sandals.
The photographer is identified on the back as "The Athenaeum Portrait Gallery. A. R. MacWilliams. Photographic Artist. 16 So. Hanover Street. (Adjoining General Post Office) Glasgow."

artworks.title: Portrait of three men wearing smoking caps
artworks.description:
Carte de visite photographic portrait of a group of three men wearing pillbox-style smoking caps. Two are seated on wooden chairs and the third stands behind and between them with a hand on a shoulder of each of the others. The standing man is wearing a dark cap, dark open coat and dark double-breasted buttoned vest. The younger man seated at left has his arms crossed and is wearing a dark cap, and light colored jacket and trousers. The man seated at the right has a lighter colored cap trimmed with braid, a dark coat left open, a light colored buttoned vest, and light colored trousers with a stripe down the side.
The photographer is identified on the back as "J. Vipond Photographer Near The Church Swine Gate, & Barrowby Lane, Grantham."

artworks.title: Portrait of father and two boys in costume
artworks.description:
Carte de visite photographic portrait of a father and two boys in costume. The father stands in the center, wearing a shirt with full sleeves gathered at the elbow, a bolero-style vest with floral and star decorations and fastened at the upper chest, and knee length pants with floral decorations down the sides. The boys stand in front on either side of him, and wear similar costumes of white close-fitting tops decorated around the necks, upper chests and cuffs with floral designs, fringe and a tassel. Their dark colored shorts have similar floral decorations. All three wear matching soft slippers with dark bows across the vamp.
The photographer is identified on the back as "James Sunderland 67, Bull Street, Birmingham".

artworks.title: Portrait of father and four children in street clothes
artworks.description:
Carte de visite photographic portrait of father and four children - one girl and three boys. All are wearing street clothes and are posed in a studio with an upholstered chair, a highly carved chest and a rectangular hassock as furnishings. The father is sitting on the chair and wearing a light colored double breasted suit. The oldest boy stands behind his left shoulder, wearing a dark jacket left open, a dark buttoned vest and a necktie with a wide flat knot. The middle son stands to the father's left and leans against the chest. His jacket is buttoned only at the top, over a buttoned vest and trousers. The youngest boy sits on his father's knee and is wearing short pants and a long sleeved top with braided trim down the front of the top, on the lower sleeves, around the bottom of the jacket, and on the sides and hem of the shorts. The curly-haired girl sits on the hassock, and is wearing a white shirt with a bow at the throat, a dark jacket trimmed on the cuffs and hem with fringed braid, and a medium-toned skirt with flounces.
The photographer is identified on the back as "T. Pope. 86. New Street. Birmingham. Opposite the Society of Artists".
See MS-0027-616-001 for image of the same boy by himself.

artworks.title: Portrait of girl in studio sitting on a rock
artworks.description:
Carte de visite photographic portrait of a girl taken in a studio with trees and mountains in the background, sitting on a rock. Her hands are folded in her lap and she is wearing an ankle-length dress with a bodice which buttons up the front, flounces on the cuffs and skirt hem, lace trimming at the cuffs, along the edge of a drape over the hips, and at the skirt hem. Her hair is pinned up, and she wears a small cap and pearl earrings.
The photographer is identified via a stamp on the back as "Albert de Lemos, successor to F. H. Bronson, Photographer 58 State Street Next to P. O. Bridgeport, Conn."

artworks.description:
Carte de visite photographic portrait of a young girl sitting side-saddle on a pony and holding the reins.. The photograph was taken outdoors, in front of a canvas tent. The fair-haired girl is wearing a light-colored knee length dress. The pony has a light-colored bridle and decorations on the crupper. The image is faded and somewhat out of focus so details are hard to discern.
There is no identification of the photographer on either the front or back of the card.

artworks.description:
Carte de visite photographic portrait of a girl with her hands folded on the corner of a table. Her dark hair is parted to the side and worn loose and brushed back. Her light-colored dress is generously trimmed with layers of small and larger flounces over the shoulders, across the middle of the bodice, at the edges of the pagoda sleeves and along the edges of various layers of drapery on the skirt. A narrow crocheted scarf is tied around her throat and there are plain undersleeves with narrow cuffs.
A handwritten notation is faintly visible on the back at the very bottom, but is mostly illegible. What can be read seems to say "E[illegible] K[illegible]nd".

artworks.title: Portrait of very young boy holding onto a trapeze
artworks.description:
Carte de visite photographic portrait of a young boy in costume, holding onto a trapeze. It is a studio portrait and he is standing in beside an upholstered and fringed stand with a striped cloth draped over the end. He is wearing a white top with ribbon trim in a deep V and a rosette at the point of the V. His shorts are trimmed with fringe in a similar V descending from the hips. The costume finishes with white tights and soft boots.
The photographer is identified on the back as "city Photograph Rooms, No. 1109 Market Street, Philadelphia. L. Horning, Operator." Note that, because of the style of the font, the L could be mistaken for J. Horning. There are also many numbers, crossed-out numbers and tick marks written on the back.

artworks.description:
Carte de visite photographic portrait of a young girl and a baby in matching dresses, posed on an upholstered chair in a carpeted studio. The older child is standing and leaning against the chair, while the baby is sitting on the chair. Their light colored dressed have dark buttons down the front although it is not clear if they are functional. There is a round neckline, short puffed sleeves and a triple row of dark ribbon running down each side of the front and around the hem of the skirt.

artworks.title: Portrait of two boys in acrobat costumes with hats
artworks.description:
Carte de visite photographic portrait of two boys in acrobatic costume, posing side by side in a studio in front of a carved panel. Both costumes include a light-colored skull cap with a vertical ruffle running back from the middle of the forehead, a skirt-like modesty garment cut in points like pennants, and soft dark boots. The boy on the left is wearing a dark long-sleeved costume divided by horizontal stripes across the chest and sleeves, with large irregular dark and light 8-pointed stars alternating across the top, sleeves and tights. The boy on the right is wearing a top and tights with vertically alternating dark and light portions in a particolored style.
Note that, while most of the costume is different, the caps are very similar to the ones worn by William Chantrell's acrobats as seen in MS-0027-606-008 and MS-0027-606-009
The photographer is identified on the back as "W. Clayton Artist & Photographer Grey Hound Street Long Row Facing Exchange Corner Late of Albert Street Nottingham".

artworks.description:

Two wear misshapen hats, and wispy facial and head hair while the third is bareheaded and his hair is more neatly trimmed. All are holding glasses of what is probably beer and all have darkened noses.
There is no information on either the front or the back about the photographer or printer.

artworks.title: Postcard photograph of woman in plain dark skirt suit
artworks.description:
Photograph printed on postcard, showing woman in simple unornamented jacket and skirt. Her bouse has a high white lace collar and a dark pleated shirt front. The cutaway jacket has white edging along the front and around the neck. It seems to come to a point so that a single button could fasten it, but the narrow knitted scarf obscures the fastener. The simple straight skirt has a pleat or seam offset to the left.
A notation in pen at bottom of the photograph is difficult to decipher but might read "Tuck A M[illegible]g.
The back is marked "Post Card" but the card was never addressed or mailed. In fact, the symbol indicating where to put the postage is partly cut off.

A net scarf is under the jacket collar and tied in a bow at the front.
The photographer is identified at the bottom front as "Smith Curry Rochester, N. Y." and a penciled notation on the back reads "Aida Reed Corse Payton show Leading Laddy[sic]".

artworks.title: Photograph of Florrie Forde
artworks.description:
Photograph of Florrie Forde sitting sideways and looking at the camera along her left shoulder. In the three-quarter length portrait she is wearing a light-colored dress with a square neckline and elbow length sleeves. There is embroidery or lace in the center of the bodice, bordered by many rows of vertical pintucks, and matching embroidery at the bottom of the sleeves. She is wearing a dark, wide-brimmed hat trimmed with feathers.
Written across the top of the image is "To Mr. & Mrs. Edie[sic]" and across the bottom below the image is "With best wishes from Florrie Forde". This bottom inscription is written over the photographer's information "From the J. P. Bamber Galleries, 103, Church St., Blackpool". Two holes are punched at the top through the backing card, presumably to be used for hanging.

artworks.description:

The draped and bustled skirt is a patterned fabric or lace.

artworks.title: Hiram Patrick Henry of Hi Henry's Minstrels
artworks.description:
Photographic portrait of man in dark jacket, dark vest, white shirt and dark bow tie. Photograph is identified on the front as "Souvenir of Hi Henry's Minstrels". There is no individual's name, but the photograph very strongly resembles a drawing identified as "Hi Henry of Hi Henry's Minstrels". This drawing appeared in the amusement section of the Oakland CA Tribune on February 25, 1899, (as reported in a blog post by Mike Brubaker https://temposenzatempo.blogspot.com/2018/03/hi-henrys-minstrels-and-big-dog.html).
The full name of the founder of this minstrel troupe is Hiram Patrick Henry (1844-1920).

artworks.title: Work & Ower, at Keith's
artworks.description:
Photograph of Work & Ower, vaudeville performers described as acrobatic comedians, or European eccentric gymnasts. The two men are standing arm in arm, dressed in what resembles but are clearly not street clothes. The figure on the left a plaid coat with very full sleeves, pants from a matching fabric with different fabric added at the bottom to make them reach the ankles, a worn hat pulled down to eyebrows, and soft laced shoes. The figure on the right is wearing an open jacket, a plaid vest, a light colored shirt with a striped tie, very long, loose chalk-striped trousers and a pork-pie hat.
They are identified on the back, with both a stamp in red ink and a penciled notation, as Work & Ower at Keith's". An additional stamp at the bottom reads "Photo Reproduced Exclusively For The Orpheum Circuit Martin Beck, General Manager".

artworks.description:

On the front below the picture, an embossed emblem identifies the manufacturer as "Milwaukee Art Novelty Co. 530 Grand Ave. Milwaukee". The back is printed with "Yamamoto Bros. Wire & Perch Artists."

artworks.title: Merrollu [sp?], clown
artworks.description:
Photographic portrait of someone costumed and with makeup of a stereotypical clown. The costume includes a white coat with large buttons down the front, a pleated collar with a shorter portion standing up around the neck and a larger portion which lays across the shoulders and a large dark bow at the throat. He wears a white skull cap hiding his hair, white facial makeup and accented lips, eyebrows and a mark between the eyebrows.
The photographer is identified on the bottom front by a gold stamped impression "Feinberg Opposite the London Theatre New York." An elaborate red emblem on the back says "Feinbert 228 Bowery, N. Y Portraits in Crayon and Pastel a Specialty. Children's pictures a great success". A penciled notation is difficult to read but seems to say "Merrollu (one of Marrollu Bros Barnum & B show".

artworks.title: Business card showing Okabe Family of Japanese acrobats and T. Okabe, manager
artworks.description:
Business card for T. Okabe, manager of the Famous Okabe Family, showing his photographic portrait bust on one side, picturing him in a medium-colored jacket, white shirt with stiff collar and a dark tie. The photograph on the reverse shows 6 men and boys in matching costumes of white tops and tights with round collars and shorts decorated with embroidery and spangles on a dark background. The smallest figure is a little girl wearing a patterned top, white tights and a skirt or sash tied in a bow at the right hip. The label beneath this picture reads "Japanese Artists".
The text on the front reads "T. Okabe" in the center. The printing at lower left says "Manager of the Famous Okabe Family and Yamagata Japanese Troupe". The printing at lower right says "Permanent Address 3019 South Park Avenue Chicago". Written in ink on this side is "Mr. Bobbio. 24 Lisle St. Leicester Sq. W. C."

artworks.title: The Great Tornados
artworks.description:
Postcard photograph of the group named The Great Tornados. A woman is sitting at center wearing a short-sleeved dress with a low-cut neckline, fringes decorating the bodice and sleeves, and large round sparkling motifs on the dress. Her hair is pinned up and she is holding flowers in her lap. Behind her is a tall woman in a light colored dress with short sleeves and cut-out motifs. Her hair is short, curled and has a large bow at the side.
The three older men are wearing cutaway coats, white vests, high collars, white bow ties and dark knickers and stockings. The youngest boy, at the left of the photograph, is dressed similarly except his vest and tie are dark.

artworks.title: Baron Giuseppe Magri, Count Primo Magri, Lavinia Warren
artworks.description:
Photograph of Baron Giuseppe (or Ernesto) Magri, Count Primo Magri and his wife Lavinia Warren, later called Countess Magri after her second marriage. The two men are wearing dark tailcoats, white vests and white bow ties. Lavinia Warren is wearing a light-colored dress with a low neckline and small puffed sleeves. Bands of contrasting trim mark the pointed waistline, the middle of the skirt and a line near the hem, and there is a rosette with trailing ribbons at the neck and the band around the middle of the skirt.
On the back is a penciled notation which reads:
Count | Marcri [sic]
Baron |
There is also a negative of the photograph which has not been scanned. Comparing the photo to the negative, it can be seen that the photo is a detail from the negative, eliminating much of the image below, above and to either side of the figures. The image is not in good focus.

artworks.title: Man leaning over bicycle
artworks.description:
Photograph, square format, showing a man with a bicycle in the yard of a house. In the background is a wooden fence, the side of a house covered in clapboards is visible to the right, and a set of wooden stairs is in the right foreground. The man is standing with his left foot on the bottom-most of the three steps, his hands on the saddle and his right leg bent as if he is stepping over the rear wheel. He is wearing a dark suit and a soft cap.
There are penciled notations on the back which seem to be a list of some sort rather than having anything to do with the photograph. They read "8 Gents 1 Ladies 1 Fur[?] 2 small".

artworks.description:
Photograph of man, unidentified, in outdoor setting. He is wearing a medium-dark suit, a white shirt with a turned-down collar and a dark bow tie. His handkerchief and the breast pocket it is in are on the wearer's right side, suggesting that the negative might have been reversed when it was printed. The image is very dark so details are difficult to discern.
The photograph is inserted into a photo holder with an oval opening, pre-printed in red, with a horseshoe surrounding the photo, the message "Good Luck from" and a blank banner at the bottom in which the sender could write a name. There are no inscriptions or notations on either the front or back.

artworks.title: Men, boys and 2 ponies at Elks Carnival, 1902
artworks.description:
Photograph, taken outdoors, of 5 men and boys with 2 ponies. A striped canvas divider supported by a wooden frame is in the background. Figures from left to right are 1) a boy wearing dark pants and jacket, white shirt, dark ribbon tie and soft cap; 2) man wearing dark pants torn at the knee with both belt and suspenders, white shirt, ribbon tie and a dark hat with taller flat crown; 3) man wearing dark jacket, vest and pants, white shirt, dark bow tie, unidentifiable hat and carries an umbrella and rolled up paper in right hand; 4) boy wearing dark jacket, striped pants, soft hat and what seems to be a rosette with trailing ribbon on his left lapel; 5) man wearing dark jacket, medium pants, checked shirt, light colored tie tucked into shirt front and boater hat. Small ponies are being held by figure #2 and figure #4.
The photograph has an unusual silver metallic looking background. The photographer is identified at the bottom front by an embossed name which reads "Holmquist Photo Co. Erie, Penna." A stamp on the back reads "Elks Carnival 1902".

artworks.title: Jumbo's body lying on ground
artworks.description:
Photograph of Jumbo the elephant after being hit by a train in St. Thomas, Canada in 1885. Jumbo is pictured lying on his left side on an embankment. There is a blurred image of his keeper standing behind Jumbo which is visible in other versions of this photograph (see MS-0027-625-007). In this copy the image of the keeper has been strengthened with pencil and the portion which was cropped out of the original has been drawn in.
There are multiple notations on the back. At the top is written "Property of Eddie F. Smith". Below that in pencil is the number "13". Next is the notation "Killed at St Thomas Canada 1885" and at lower left it says "Property of E. Fritz Smith 107 York Ave". Lastly across the right hand end is written "Jumbo was killed at Thomas Canada 1885".

artworks.description:
Cabinet card studio photograph of Ernie Stanton costumed as a rooster. The costume imitates a very realistic rooster using real feathers, fabric in place of wattles and comb, and shoes which look like chicken feet. He is standing next to an ornamental pedestal with a piece of ceramic resting on top.
AT the bottom front the photographer is identified as "White 1261 Broadway. 105 Fourth Ave. N.Y." Penciled notations on the back read No 7. Ernie Stanton as Rooster Feb 25 1904".

artworks.description:

artworks.title: Ernie Stanton as a Chicken, Fritz Smith in clown costume
artworks.description:
Photograph of person costumed as a chicken with dark feathers standing with a person costumed as a clown. The clown is wearing a costume with a high-waisted medium colored top, long sleeves gathered at the wrists with cuffs made from striped fabric, and a wide round collar. The top is attached to very full pants made from the same horizontally striped fabric as the cuffs. He is holding a shallow basket as if to feed the chicken. Behind the two figures is a table covered with a cloth. Near the bottom of the cloth, between the chicken and the clown, is visible "#73". That seems to have been part of the image before this was printed rather than written directly on the photograph.
Handwritten notations on the back read "Fritz Smith & Walter Stanton 1887" and "10". A sticker on the back reads "W. N. Sweet Photographic Expert. Interior, Commercial and and [sic] all Difficult Work a Specialty. Duplicates of these Photos can be had by addressing W. N. Sweet, Chicago, Ill. Care Sweet, Wallach & Co., 229 and 231 State St."

The photograph was taken on a dirt road in front of an open field with a house and other buildings on the horizon. This copy is broken in two with the break running from top to bottom slightly to the right of center. Cellophane tape was used on the front and back to hold the pieces together.
Written on the back: "The Gentry Bros Famous Shows United J. W. Gentrys No 2. "The Boys Hussar Band." taken on May 10th Tuesday - 04. at Alexandra Ind. Also Edwin Fritz the Clown and Pantomimist who was working with Walter Stanton Giant Rooster Act."

artworks.title: Cottonwood Lake, Utah
artworks.description:
Photograph, carte de visite, of a lake in the mountains of Utah. Several figures are visible on a raft in a body of water. Some bushes are visible on the ground and bare tree branches extend into the field of view from the upper right in the near foreground. In the near background are tree-covered slopes while a pointed peak is visible in the far distance.
An imprint on the back identifying the photographer reads "C. R. Savage, (Late Savage & Ottinger,) Pioneer Art Gallery, East Temple Street, Salt Lake City. Utah. Portrait and Landscape Photography in All Its Branches. Views of Every Point of Interest in the Great West: A penciled notation at the side reads "Cottonwood Lake Utah".
Per information on the Brigham Young University Library web site (https://lib.byu.edu/collections/c-r-savage-collection/about/), Charles Roscoe Savage was born in England in 1832, immigrated to New York in 1856 where he became interested in establishing a photography business, moved to locations in Nebraska, and arrived with his family in Salt Lake City, Utah in 1860. two separate fires in his Art Bazaar, on 26 June 1883 and in 1911 after his death destroyed all his negatives.

artworks.title: View of Salt Lake City from top of Temple
artworks.description:
Photograph, cabinet card, showing view across Salt Lake City from the top of the Temple. Two three-story buildings with multiple extensions and outbuildings are visible at lower center with similar but smaller buildings facing them across the road which slants from lower right to middle left. Behind the smaller buldings is a large long industrial building. Further to left along the road, near the edge of the photograph, is a large Italianate style house in a neighborhood of some similar style houses. More of the city is visible in the background.
The photograph is somewhat faded.
A hand-written note at the bottom left of the image reads "S. L. City From Top of Temple." An imprint on the back reads "F. I. Monsen & Co. Photographers, Salt Lake City, Utah."

artworks.title: Cornalla & Eddie with plant stand
artworks.description:
Postcard, studio photograph of Don G. Cornalla and Eddie F. Smith as if performing. Cornalla stands at left with his fists on his hips, wearing a dark single-breasted suit, a white shirt, a white cravat and a straight tie pin. A two-color handkerchief folded into points is tucked in his breast pocket. Eddie is in his usual clown makeup and hair and is wearing a white shirt with an over-large white bow tie, very long baggy dark pants held up by white suspenders and a very large dark garment which might be meant resemble a vest. One leg of a 3-legged piece of furniture has been snagged in the vest.
The photographers are identified on the back as "Relph & Co., Photographers, 130A Church Street. Preston". The undivided postcard back is imprinted at top "Relph's Post Card Series (Preston)". Below that is "For 1/2 d. Postage only Name and Address is permitted. If any other Writing, Letter Postage should be paid." artworks.title: Cornalla & Eddie with umbrella
artworks.description:
Postcard, studio photograph of Don G. Cornalla and Eddie F. Smith. Cornalla stands at left, wearing a dark single-breasted suit, a white shirt, a white cravat and a straight tie pin. Eddie is in his usual clown makeup and hair and is wearing a white shirt with an over-large white bow tie, very long baggy dark pants and suit jacket, and extremely large white gloves. Cornalla is holding Eddie's dark top hat as if he just took it off Eddie's head, and they each have their right hand on a rolled-up umbrella.
There is a penciled notation on the back which reads "Uncle Eddie". The photographers are identified on the back as "Relph & Co., Photographers, 130A Church Street. Preston". The undivided postcard back is imprinted at top "Relph's Post Card Series (Preston)". Below that is "For 1/2 d. Postage only Name and Address is permitted. If any other Writing, Letter Postage should be paid." In the upper right corner where stamps are usually applied is a square outline containing the imprint "L A Here". Note that the L and A are overlapping so that the base of the L forms the cross-bar of the A.

An embossed emblem at the bottom right in the form of a circle with rectangle superimposed also identifies the studio as "Craely Metropole Studios Cardiff". artworks.description:

artworks.title: Paul Gorden, American Wire Wunder
artworks.description:
Photograph, Paul Gorden American Wire Wunder [sic]. The image shows him walking on a wire, wearing a dark knee-length coat, dark pants, a white shirt, patterned tie and top hat. He is holding a liquor bottle in his right hand, waving with his left hand, and in a slightly slumped posture perhaps meant to suggest that he is inebriated. Printed in an arc above his head is "Paul Gorden American Wire Wunder [sic]".
A debossed logo at the lower left front identifies the photographer as "The Murmann Studio 3, Gresham Road, Brixton. S.W." On the back a penciled inscription repeats the text from the front except for the change from German to English spelling for Wonder "Paul Gorden American Wire Wonder". An isolated letter G appears further to the right. Near the bottom is penciled "Grösse 9 x 14 cm" while at the bottom right is "#1436."

artworks.title: W. C. Fields
artworks.description:
Photograph, studio portrait, of W. C. Fields in costume. He is wearing asuit including a relatively long dark jacket left open, matching pleated front pants, a single-breasted three button vest cut with a low U-shaped neckline, and a white shirt with a pointed collar. His tie seems to be a dark ribbon with a light-colored stripe along either side, tied with a knot at the throat and the ends left short and loose. He is wearing a battered dark top hat, and is holding a skinny curved bamboo cane in his right hand a a pair of worn gloves in his left hand.
At the bottom right corner of the front is a photographer's emblem in the form of a red rosette with a lighter red circular center and the name "Campbell Gray 17 Cheapside E. C." An inscription on the back reads "With Best Wishes to Eddie W. C. Fields 1913". A partial inscription remains at the bottom left reading "[missing] Hart".

artworks.title: Annie Ferguson
artworks.description:

She is wearing a light colored, high-necked long sleeved dress with narrow vertical tucks above the bust, wider vertical tucks on the lower front and horizontal tucks at the sides. There is lace trim on the collar and bodice, small earrings, a short necklace and a pin for jewelry, and she is wearing a hat trimmed with similar-colored flowers.
An inscription at the bottom front reads " To Mrs. B. [sic] Eddie from A Pal, Annie Ferguson". There are no inscriptions or marks on the back.

artworks.title: Nick Hufford, minstrel
artworks.description:
Photograph, studio portrait bust of Nick Hufford (Nicodemus David Hufford II, 21 Sep 1884 - 26 July 1956), minstrel and vaudeville comedian. In the oval photograph he is wearing a double-breasted jacket in a dark plaid fabric with wide lapels, light colored shirt with a high collar and turned-down collar points, and a light colored tie with small geometric motifs. An inscription at lower right front reads "Truly Yours, Nick Hufford. c/o Al. G. F. Minstrels To Eddie." and is dated "Apr. 26 1905."
See this entry (https://www.loc.gov/item/2014636979/) in the Library of Congress for a poster showing Nick Hufford as part of the Al. G. Field Minstrels.
The photographer is identified by an embossed emblem at bottom right. It is difficult to read because the inscription is written over the emblem, but seems to read "Good & Kushner 4 1/2 S. High St."

artworks.title: Ella Shields
artworks.description:
Photograph, full length studio portrait of Ella Shields, music hall singer and male impersonator. She is posing with her hands behind her back, her head slightly turned and looking at the camera with a smiling cheerful look on her face. She is wearing a high-waisted, high necked, light colored dress with various patterns of lace decorating the bodice, the oversleeves and the elbow length undersleeves. The underskirt is plain and separate lace panels overlay it. Tassels hang from the raised waist and from each sleeve.
An inscription appears in two parts at the upper left and lower right of the front reading "With Love to Buelah [sic] Sincerely Ella Shields /08". The photographer is identified at lower right at "S. Langfier 137. Sauchiehall St. Glasgow".

Their daughter Tottie is standing behind him wearing a dress which buttons up the left front and has a close-fitting square neckline and elbow-length sleeves, both trimmed with matching rows of dark-and-light trim.

artworks.title: "The 2 Bobs"
artworks.description:
Photograph of two men in street clothes. Both are wearing dark suits. The one in front, to the viewer's left is wearing a striped shirt and dark tie with polka dots and is standing with his hands in his pockets. The second stands slightly behind and to his left, looking over the shoulder of the first and pointing toward the camera.
There is an inscription across the lower portion of the image. Because of the black ink on the dark image, parts are difficult to read. It seems to say "To Little 'Eddie' Smith Bradfords friend, [sincerely?] Bob [iillegible] Adams" On the back an inscription says "The 2 Bobs first to introduce Rag time in England".
A stamp in one corner of the back, oriented upside down to the inscription, is also only partially legible. It seems to read "The 'Velvograph' Panel Frank Dobson [illegible] Liverpool"

artworks.description:

His costume includes a pillbox-style hat and a jacket or shirt with a wide collar.
On the front is an inscription in ink reading "From one Tramp to the other Joe Ho Educi". The photographer is identified by a white signature at bottom right as Joe Jackson.

artworks.title: "Mr." McCloud in Scottish attire
artworks.description:
Photograph of a figure dressed in Scottish kilt and regalia. They are wearing a dark jacket with satin lapels, and braid and diamond-shaped buttons trimming the cuffs and pockets. The kilt is a plain dark fabric, the vest is a plain light color and the shirt has a high collar and lace jabot. A "plaid" made of dark tartan fabric is pinned to the left shoulder. They are wearing a sporran with a metal frame and white and dark horsehair trim. A large soft beret is ornamented with a metal cap badge and feather. Dark socks reach to the calf and the shoes are flat, ornamented with a buckle and tied around the ankles.
The photographer is identified on the front at bottom left as "Rembrandt 1364 B'way N Y." A penciled notation on the back seems to read "Mr. McCloud".

artworks.description:

artworks.title: Two Rascals & Jacobson - Eddie Fields, Charles O'Donnell, Jesse Jacobson
artworks.description:
Photograph, studio image also used as publicity photo for jazz and ragtime singers and musicians Two Rascals & Jacobson, including Eddie Fields (Edward Greenfield, 1894-1962), Charles O'Donnell (1888-1951) and Jesse Jacobson (1882-1959). All three are wearing matching dark jackets, white shirts with wing-tip collars and white bow ties.
All parts of the ink inscription are on the front. The portion of the inscription at upper left reads "To 'Shrimp' Eddie The boy wonder from "I a may." From left to fright, the names written on each individual read "Eddie", "Jes." and "Chas." Below the image an inscription reads "Every good wish. Two Rascals & Jacobson. Jan. 28 1916"
See the article Hedges Brothers and Jacobson: Ragtime Invaders (chrome-extension://efaidnbmnnnibpcajpcglclefindmkaj/https://www.vjm.biz/172-hedges-bros-web-res.pdf) by Bruce Vermazen in the Vintage Jazz Mart for additional information.

artworks.title: Charles S. Stratton's Court Suit, 1844
artworks.description:
Miniature court suit made of brown silk velvet, probably mid-1840s or 1850s, worn by Charles S. Stratton, a little person better known by his stage name General Tom Thumb. The suit consists of a fitted, cutaway tailcoat and breeches with faceted cut steel buttons. The pale gold satin lining is not original to the garment. A fine white linen shirt with ruffled front would have been worn with the jacket, and white silk stockings with the breeches.
Stratton was a performer who worked for the showman P. T. Barnum, and Stratton played a variety of character roles for which he had different costumes. This suit may be one of his costumes, or it may have been worn in the Royal court, when he was introduced to Queen Victoria while touring the British Isles with Barnum.

artworks.title: "M'lle Jenny Lind's Grand Concert"
artworks.description:
Ticket for M'lle [Mademoiselle] Jenny Lind's Grand Concert printed in black ink on red cardstock, dating to either 1850 or 1851, with a decorative border around the text. This ticket dates from Jenny Lind’s immensely successful American tour from 1850 to 1851. It is unknown which concert this ticket was issued for, however the red color indicates it was made after Barnum instituted a color coded system of seating to help manage the large crowds who came to hear the famed soprano, popularly known as "The Swedish Nightingale." P. T. Barnum's embossed seal appears in the lower left corner over the text that reads "admit one." On the right lower corner is his signature. In the lower margin, is the name and address of the printer: "Van Norden & Amerman, Printers, 60 William street, New York." A statement on the reverse side advises the ticket holder to buy his or her program before sitting down, since "it is impossible to supply the same after the audience are seated," and noting that "The only AUTHORIZED EDITION is sold in the entrance and in the house."
Lind arrived in New York City on September 11, 1850 for a year-long tour of North America. At the time, Lind was relatively unknown in the United States since few Americans were familiar with opera, but Barnum heavily promoted her in advance of her arrival, creating high demand for concert tickets, some of which were auctioned at very high prices. Manufacturers quickly capitalized on the public's adoration of Lind and produced innumerable consumer products bearing her likeness or name; the desire for all things "Jenny" was called "Lind-mania."
